column1: # exemptions.tsv — every exemption a check makes, with a reason and an end date.
# A rule without exceptions is a rule people route around; an exception nobody
# wrote down is a rule that quietly stopped applying. A hard-coded exemption
# list inside a check has no reason and no end date, so it goes stale unseen: a
# file moves, a sibling is added, and the stale list still looks like the guard
# working. Keeping every exemption here, with both, makes that visible.
#   check    which check reads the row (its own name, no path)
#   pattern  what to exempt; each check interprets this in its own terms
#            (check-em-dash: a regex of text that is not prose;
#             check-space-boundary: a path prefix of a file allowed to carry
#             the literals the guard hunts for)
#   reason   why. Required. Write it for the person who finds this in a year.
# "structural" is not a waiver. It marks a case where the rule was stated too
# broadly and this row is part of its real definition, so there is nothing to
# come back to. Anything that is a temporary allowance gets a date, and
# check-exemptions reports it as OVERDUE once that date passes.

column4: reason

A long CLI flag is not prose. The ban is on punctuation a reader sees as a dash; --no-verify and --dry-run are code that happens to live in a sentence. Without it, a commit message that names a flag is refused for punctuation it does not contain.
The guard necessarily contains the literals it searches for, in its own patterns and comments. It cannot be made to not match itself.
Exercises the guard, so it contains the same literals on purpose.

Scaffolds a real space in the real vault for the length of its run (see its header), so during that window the fixture owner is a genuine passport entry and the guard finds the literal again in the test that created it.
Carries the literals it detects in its own patterns, for the same reason as the guard itself.

A minified vendor bundle is not authored text. Invisible characters in it belong to the library that shipped them, and the rule is about characters smuggled into prose a human wrote. Rewriting a vendored bundle to satisfy a content check corrupts it.

This script IS the loader for its own run. It reaches a machine through curl into bash, before the repository exists, so it inlines the nvm and Homebrew probing that _toolpaths.sh does rather than sourcing a file that is not there yet.

This tool relocates the user's real installation and rewrites the agent pointers in their actual home. AGENTBRAIN_HOME would send it at a sandbox and leave the machine untouched, which is the opposite of what it is for.

The offending lines sit inside heredocs: this negative case writes a deliberately wrong script to prove the trap guard catches it. The literal is test data, never a path this repo resolves, so no sandbox can escape through it.

The negative case writes throwaway scripts containing the exact hardcoded vault path the trap guard must catch. Quoting the defect is what proves the guard fires, so this file will always hold it; there is nothing to come back to.
Migration rewrites the checkout symlink itself; it must inspect the checkout path, not resolve vault contents.
Migration checks whether the checkout has a vault symlink; it does not read vault content.
Adopted code credited to ultimate_tagger with no upstream URL and no licence anywhere in the addon. Ask the author or replace it; the add-on is small enough to rewrite.
The README says to check the upstream LICENSE before redistribution, and that check is still open. No upstream code ships, so the risk is low; the answer is one visit to the upstream repository root.

The delimiters of an HTML comment are markup, not punctuation. Both carry two hyphens by syntax and neither can be written another way. Only the delimiters are stripped: a real "--" inside the comment text still trips the check. Matching the whole comment instead does not work, because the stripper runs with re.M and not re.S, so a multi-line comment is never matched. Vendored files carry <!-- PROVENANCE comments, and each would trip on its next edit.
The rule that settles the local/ identity spelling has to name that spelling to explain it.
Vendored skills: their paths name files in the upstream repository they were copied from, not in this one.
Vendored skill: its README names files in the upstream repository.
These skills write documents into the reader's own project; docs/ and scripts/ there are that project's folders.
The add-on works on the reader's own repository; docs/ there is that repository's folder.
A template contract: templates/ is relative to the generated infographic project.
Templates for a distilled repository: docs/ and system/ name folders of the repository being distilled.
The spec names a gate runner and key directory as worked examples and backlog, not as shipped files.
Templates and examples for a new add-on: the paths name the add-on the reader is about to create.
